newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan tightens rules on rights issue pricing.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan tightens rules on rights issue pricing.

text.p: Taiwan regulators mandated on Tuesday that listed firms set their rights issue underwriting prices near their shares' market price to maximise funds raised and avoid handing excessive profits to big shareholders.

The Securities and Exchange Commission said it revised its rules to mandate that rights issue shares be priced above 90 percent of the underlying shares' average market price in the past 10, 20 or 30 days for book building or book running.
For rights issues issued through lotteries, the price must be above 70 percent of the firm's average market price in the past 10, 20 or 30 days, a commission official told Reuters.
The revision has immediate effect and aims to limit the excessive profits of major shareholders, the official said.
"This move is to allow listed firms raise more funds in their rights issue and to avoid big shareholders from taking excess profits," she said.

Typically, prices of book building rights issues have ranged around 70-80 percent of the underlying share's average price, while for those issued through lotteries the prices have been about 50-60 percent, the official said.
Rights issue prices in Taiwan are set with a premium over their shares' par value, or T$10 per share.
The change applies to firms listed in the main Taiwan Stock Exchange and the over-the-counter market, the official said.
Analysts said the move could dampen investors' willingness to buy rights issues due to the higher pricing.
"While listed firms can raise more funds from the new move, investors in general may be less interested in buying their rights issue from now on," said National Securities manager Allen Huang.
